payload.snippet: Sugar and flour need measuring.
options: Use the measuring cups
Guess with a handful
Use a toy cup
Pour the whole bag in
payload.explanation: Measuring cups give the right amounts.

payload.snippet: The muffins are too hot to eat.
options: Wait for them to cool down
Blow on them and eat immediately
Put them in the freezer for one second
Eat them straight from the tin
payload.explanation: Hot food needs time to cool.

payload.snippet: The recipe says crack two eggs.
options: Crack them on the bowl edge gently
Smash them on the floor
Drop them from high up
Squeeze them until they break
payload.explanation: Gentle cracking keeps shell out of the batter.

payload.snippet: Ben's sister wants to help sprinkle icing.
options: Let her have a turn
Pour all the icing on at once himself
Tell her she will do it wrong
Run away with the icing bag
payload.explanation: Sharing baking tasks is fun for everyone.

payload.snippet: The dough is too sticky to roll.
options: Add a little flour to the board
Add water to make it stickier
Throw it in the bin
Hit it with a rolling pin very hard
payload.explanation: A dusting of flour prevents dough from sticking.

payload.snippet: The timer goes off but the cake looks pale.
options: Ask a grown-up to check if it needs more time
Take it out because the timer said so
Put it on full heat for one minute
Eat the pale cake anyway
payload.explanation: Timers are a guide — an adult checks doneness properly.

payload.snippet: Lily wants to try the batter.
options: Ask Mum if it is safe to taste first
Eat a big spoonful straight away
Give some to the dog
Eat it while no one is looking
payload.explanation: Some batters contain raw egg — always ask an adult before tasting.

payload.snippet: The chocolate chips need melting.
options: Ask a grown-up to help melt them safely
Put them in the oven while it is very hot
Melt them over a flame alone
Eat them all before melting
payload.explanation: Melting chocolate needs adult supervision.

payload.snippet: Tom gets flour on the kitchen counter.
options: Wipe it up with a damp cloth
Blow it across the room
Leave it for someone else
Sweep it onto the floor
payload.explanation: Cleaning up as you go keeps the kitchen safe.

payload.snippet: The cake is stuck in the tin.
options: Use a blunt knife around the edges first
Pull it out hard from one side
Shake the tin upside down violently
Eat it straight from the tin
payload.explanation: Loosening edges before turning out a cake prevents it breaking.

payload.snippet: The dough needs kneading for five minutes.
options: Push and fold the dough rhythmically
Throw it against the wall
Stand on it
Leave it alone and hope it kneads itself
payload.explanation: Rhythmic kneading develops the gluten structure in bread dough.

payload.snippet: Zoe wants to decorate the cupcakes.
options: Spread the icing on with a spoon or knife
Squirt it directly from the tube at her brother
Put all the sprinkles on one cupcake
Eat the icing before decorating
payload.explanation: Spreading icing evenly makes every cupcake look good.

payload.snippet: The recipe asks for a pinch of salt.
options: Use two fingers to pick up a tiny amount
Pour the whole salt shaker in
Skip the salt since it is a tiny amount
Use a teaspoon of salt instead
payload.explanation: A pinch means a tiny amount between two fingertips.

payload.snippet: The brownies need cooling before cutting.
options: Wait until they are completely cool
Cut them while hot and they crumble
Put them straight in the fridge for one minute
Eat them from the tray with a fork
payload.explanation: Warm brownies crumble when cut — cooling makes clean squares.

payload.snippet: Sam spills milk while measuring it.
options: Wipe it up right away before it spreads
Leave it and see if it dries
Walk through it
Tell no one
payload.explanation: Spills cleaned immediately prevent slipping and sticky residues.

payload.snippet: Mia wants to plant a seed.
options: Dig a small hole with her finger
Throw the seed on the ground
Plant it upside down in the air
Put it on the shelf
payload.explanation: Seeds need to be in soil to grow.

payload.snippet: The seedling needs water.
options: Use a small watering can
Pour a bucket over it
Throw water from far away
Use a hose on full power
payload.explanation: Gentle watering with a small can doesn't flatten seedlings.

payload.snippet: Tom's pot plant is dry.
options: Check the soil with a finger first
Pour lots of water in quickly
Leave it in the rain only
Give it juice instead of water
payload.explanation: Checking the soil prevents overwatering.

payload.snippet: A seed packet says plant in spring.
options: Wait until spring to plant it
Plant it in winter frost
Plant it in summer heat
Plant it whenever you feel like it
payload.explanation: Seeds grow best when planted at the right season.

payload.snippet: The flower pot has no drainage holes.
options: Ask an adult to make some holes
Fill the pot with rocks instead of soil
Use it without holes anyway
Use a bucket instead
payload.explanation: Drainage holes prevent roots from sitting in water.

payload.snippet: Lily puts too much soil in the pot.
options: Remove some so the plant has room to grow
Push the plant down hard
Add more soil on top
Use a bigger plant instead
payload.explanation: Plants need space to grow in their pots.

payload.snippet: A plant's leaves are turning yellow.
options: Ask a grown-up what is wrong
Pull the yellow leaves off
Water it more
Put it in the dark
payload.explanation: Yellow leaves can mean different things — an adult can help diagnose.

payload.snippet: Ben finds a worm in the garden soil.
options: Leave it alone — it helps the garden
Pull it out and throw it away
Pour salt on it
Put it in the flower pot inside
payload.explanation: Worms improve soil by aerating it.

payload.snippet: The seeds need labelling.
options: Write the plant name on a lolly stick
Guess which is which after planting
Remember them without labelling
Draw a tiny picture on each seed
payload.explanation: Labels help you remember what you planted.

payload.snippet: A sunflower is growing too big for its small pot.
options: Move it to a bigger pot or the garden
Cut the roots to make it fit
Tie the roots into the pot
Put a lid on the top of the pot
payload.explanation: Plants need space for roots to grow.

payload.snippet: Zoe's herb pot has no sunlight.
options: Move it to the sunniest windowsill
Buy a lamp for the herbs
Paint the walls white to reflect light
Give it extra water instead
payload.explanation: Most herbs need sunlight to grow well.

payload.snippet: The soil in the garden feels very hard.
options: Add water and let it soften
Stamp on it to break it up
Use a kitchen knife to cut it
Leave the seeds on top of hard soil
payload.explanation: Softening soil first helps seeds to germinate.

payload.snippet: A carrot is ready to pull from the ground.
options: Pull it gently and straight
Grab it and yank hard from one side
Dig it out with a spade roughly
Cut the top off and leave the rest underground
payload.explanation: Gentle straight pulling avoids breaking the carrot.

payload.snippet: Sam's seedlings are very crowded in the tray.
options: Thin them out so each has space
Leave them crowded — the strongest will survive
Water them more to make space
Pull out all but one seedling
payload.explanation: Thinning seedlings gives the strongest ones room to grow.

payload.snippet: A new plant needs staking because it is leaning.
options: Tie it gently to a bamboo cane
Push it upright with your hands every day
Lean a brick against it
Leave it leaning until it falls over
payload.explanation: Staking supports weak or tall plants.

payload.snippet: The lawn is long and needs mowing.
options: Tell a grown-up the grass needs cutting
Use the garden scissors
Cut it with kitchen scissors
Pull each blade of grass by hand
payload.explanation: Lawn mowers are adult tools — tell an adult when the grass is long.

payload.snippet: Ella plants a seed but nothing grows after two weeks.
options: Read the packet to check how long it takes
Dig it up to check
Plant ten more seeds on top
Throw the whole pot away
payload.explanation: Some seeds take many weeks to germinate — check the packet.

payload.snippet: A slug is eating the lettuce leaves.
options: Tell a grown-up who can put down slug pellets safely
Squash it with your foot
Pour salt directly on the lettuce
Spray the plant with washing-up liquid
payload.explanation: Slug control needs adult guidance to be safe for the plant.

payload.snippet: Oscar waters his plant but the water runs straight through the pot.
options: Check whether the soil has become very dry and compacted
Water it again ten minutes later
Add more soil on top
Put the plant in a bucket of water to soak
payload.explanation: Water running straight through can mean the soil is too dry to absorb — soaking is sometimes needed.

payload.snippet: The plant is getting too much sun and the leaves look scorched.
options: Move it to a spot with indirect light
Water it more to cool it down
Cover it with a cloth all day
Leave it since sunlight is always good for plants
payload.explanation: Some plants prefer indirect light — scorched leaves signal too much direct sun.

payload.snippet: The dog's water bowl is empty.
options: Fill it with fresh water
Give the dog juice
Leave it empty
Fill it with milk
payload.explanation: Dogs need fresh water available all the time to stay healthy.

payload.snippet: The cat is scratching at the litter box.
options: Clean out the litter box
Shoo the cat away
Fill the box with water
Move the box outside
payload.explanation: A dirty litter box makes cats uncomfortable; cleaning it keeps them happy.

payload.snippet: The hamster wheel is squeaking loudly.
options: Put a tiny drop of oil on the axle
Take the wheel away
Wake the hamster up
Stuff the wheel with tissue
payload.explanation: A little oil stops the squeak so the hamster can run quietly at night.

payload.snippet: The fish tank is getting cloudy.
options: Do a partial water change
Add more fish food
Turn off the filter
Cover the tank with a cloth
payload.explanation: Changing part of the water removes waste and keeps the fish healthy.

payload.snippet: The puppy is whining by the door.
options: Take the puppy outside for a walk
Give the puppy a treat
Ignore the puppy
Let the puppy into the kitchen
payload.explanation: Puppies whine at the door when they need to go to the toilet or want exercise.

payload.snippet: The cat knocks its food bowl off the shelf.
options: Pick up the bowl and refill it at floor level
Leave the food on the floor
Put the cat outside
Move the bowl to a higher shelf
payload.explanation: Food bowls belong on the floor so cats can eat safely.

payload.snippet: The rabbit's hay rack is empty.
options: Fill the rack with fresh hay
Give the rabbit biscuits
Leave the rack empty
Replace hay with lettuce only
payload.explanation: Rabbits need unlimited hay every day for their digestion.

payload.snippet: The dog's fur is matted and tangled.
options: Gently brush the dog's coat
Cut all the fur off
Wash the dog in the pond
Leave the tangles
payload.explanation: Regular brushing removes tangles and keeps a dog's coat healthy.

payload.snippet: The bird's cage is very dirty.
options: Clean the cage with warm water
Add more food to cover the dirt
Move the bird to a box
Leave the cage dirty
payload.explanation: A clean cage keeps birds healthy and free from disease.

payload.snippet: The guinea pig squeaks and runs to its food bowl.
options: Give the guinea pig fresh vegetables
Tap the cage to calm it down
Add bedding to its bowl
Ignore the squeaking
payload.explanation: Guinea pigs squeak when they are hungry; fresh vegetables are a healthy treat.

payload.snippet: The dog is limping on one front paw.
options: Check the paw for a thorn or cut
Make the dog run to stretch it out
Put a bandage on without looking
Leave it to heal on its own today
payload.explanation: A limp often means something is hurting; checking the paw finds thorns or injuries quickly.

payload.snippet: The cat is sick after eating something outside.
options: Keep the cat calm indoors and call the vet
Give the cat more food to settle its stomach
Let the cat back outside
Put the cat in a bath
payload.explanation: If a cat has eaten something harmful, a vet can advise on the safest next steps.

payload.snippet: The goldfish is swimming sideways near the surface.
options: Test the water quality and call a pet shop for advice
Add extra fish food
Change all the water at once
Take the fish out and put it in a cup
payload.explanation: Sideways swimming usually signals a water quality problem or swim bladder issue; advice before acting prevents further harm.

payload.snippet: The puppy chews on an electrical cable.
options: Gently redirect the puppy to a chew toy and cover the cable
Shout loudly at the puppy
Put the puppy in another room all day
Wrap the cable in tape and leave it
payload.explanation: Puppies chew instinctively; redirecting to safe toys protects both the pup and the home.

payload.snippet: The rabbit has escaped from its hutch into the garden.
options: Move slowly and calmly to herd the rabbit back into a safe enclosure
Chase the rabbit around the garden quickly
Leave the rabbit outside overnight
Call the rabbit loudly from indoors
payload.explanation: Rabbits panic easily; slow, calm movement prevents injury and makes recapture easier.

payload.snippet: The dog refuses to eat its food for two days.
options: Take the dog to the vet for a check-up
Switch to a completely new food right away
Give the dog human leftovers to tempt it
Reduce the portion size and see if it eats less
payload.explanation: Two days without eating is a sign something may be wrong; a vet check rules out illness.

payload.snippet: The cat's claws are getting very long.
options: Trim the claws with special pet nail clippers
File the claws with a nail file
Let the cat scratch on the furniture
Cover the cat's paws with socks
payload.explanation: Regular claw trimming prevents the claws curling into the paw pads, which is very painful.

payload.snippet: The hamster has not come out of its nest for two days.
options: Check that the hamster is still eating and drinking; if not, consult a vet
Move all the bedding to find it
Shine a bright torch into the nest
Shake the cage gently to wake it
payload.explanation: Hamsters sleep a lot but should still eat and drink; a vet call is wise if signs of life are absent.

payload.snippet: The dog is scratching its ears constantly.
options: Examine the ear for redness or smell and visit the vet
Pour water into the ear to soothe it
Ignore it for a few weeks
Give the dog a bath and hope it clears
payload.explanation: Persistent ear scratching often means infection or ear mites, which need veterinary treatment.

payload.snippet: The pet tortoise has not moved or eaten for three days in winter.
options: Check the temperature of the enclosure and ensure it is warm enough
Give the tortoise a cold bath to wake it
Move the tortoise to the garden
Offer the tortoise meat to increase its energy
payload.explanation: Tortoises slow down dramatically if they are cold; maintaining the correct temperature range keeps them active and eating.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour's ball rolls into your garden.
options: Take the ball back to your neighbour
Keep the ball
Kick it over the fence
Hide it in the shed
payload.explanation: Returning something that belongs to someone else is the kind thing to do.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour looks sad sitting on the doorstep.
options: Say hello and ask if they are okay
Ignore them and go inside
Run away
Wave and hurry past
payload.explanation: Noticing when someone is sad and checking on them is being a good neighbour.

payload.snippet: The elderly lady next door is carrying heavy shopping bags.
options: Offer to carry the bags for her
Walk straight past her
Tell her to use a trolley
Take one bag without asking
payload.explanation: Helping with heavy loads is a kind and thoughtful thing to do.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour's dog has escaped through the garden fence.
options: Tell your neighbour straight away
Chase the dog yourself
Ignore it and go inside
Close your own gate and do nothing
payload.explanation: Letting the owner know quickly is the safest way to help get the dog back.

payload.snippet: The baby next door is crying very loudly late at night.
options: Leave it to the parents to handle
Knock on the door at midnight
Shout through the wall
Call the police immediately
payload.explanation: Babies cry — parents know what to do. Knocking late at night would disturb everyone.

payload.snippet: You see your neighbour drop their keys and keep walking.
options: Pick up the keys and call out to them
Keep the keys
Leave them on the ground
Put them through a random letterbox
payload.explanation: Calling out and returning dropped keys is a helpful and honest thing to do.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour's washing has blown off the line into your garden.
options: Hand the laundry back over the fence
Keep the clothes
Leave them on the wet ground
Put them in your bin
payload.explanation: Returning things that blow into your garden is a neighbourly and honest act.

payload.snippet: A new family moves in next door with a child your age.
options: Smile and say hello when you see them
Stare at them and say nothing
Tell them to go away
Run inside and hide
payload.explanation: Welcoming new neighbours with a friendly hello helps them feel at home.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour's cat is stuck up a tree.
options: Tell your neighbour so they can help
Try to climb the tree yourself
Shout loudly at the cat
Walk away and forget about it
payload.explanation: Telling the owner is the safest first step — they can decide how to help.

payload.snippet: You accidentally kick your ball through your neighbour's window.
options: Tell your parent and go apologise straight away
Run inside and pretend it wasn't you
Blame someone else
Wait to see if they notice
payload.explanation: Owning up to accidents quickly is always the right thing to do.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour asks you not to play loud music near their window while their baby sleeps.
options: Move further away or play more quietly
Turn the music up louder
Argue that you were there first
Play music anyway because it's your garden
payload.explanation: Being considerate of others' needs, especially babies sleeping, is good neighbourly behaviour.

payload.snippet: The man next door slips on ice at the bottom of his steps.
options: Ask if he is hurt and tell your parent
Laugh and go inside
Walk past without saying anything
Tell him he should have been more careful
payload.explanation: Checking if someone is hurt and getting a grown-up is the caring and sensible thing to do.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour leaves a note asking you to keep the shared path clear of bikes.
options: Move your bike and say thank you for letting you know
Leave the bikes where they are
Take down the note and ignore it
Write a rude reply
payload.explanation: Respecting shared spaces and being gracious about polite requests keeps neighbours happy.

payload.snippet: You notice the lights in the house next door have been on all night and no one has opened the curtains.
options: Mention it to a parent or trusted adult
Ring the doorbell every hour
Break a window to check inside
Ignore it completely
payload.explanation: Mentioning an unusual observation to a trusted adult is the safe and sensible action.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour grows prize roses and you accidentally break one off playing in the garden.
options: Tell your parent and offer to apologise to the neighbour
Push the broken flower back into the soil
Throw it away and say nothing
Blame the wind
payload.explanation: Honesty and offering an apology shows responsibility and earns respect.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour brings home-baked biscuits to your door as a thank-you for helping them.
options: Say thank you warmly and share them with your family
Say you don't want them and close the door
Take them without saying anything
Give them back and say you don't eat biscuits
payload.explanation: Accepting a kind gift graciously and saying thank you makes the other person feel appreciated.

payload.snippet: A parcel is delivered to your house that is addressed to your neighbour.
options: Bring the parcel next door as soon as possible
Open it to see what's inside
Leave it outside in the rain
Keep it and say nothing
payload.explanation: Returning a wrongly delivered parcel quickly is honest and considerate.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour is away on holiday and their wheelie bin is blocking the shared path.
options: Move the bin to the side so people can pass
Leave it blocking the path — not your problem
Tip the bin over
Go through their garden to move it further away
payload.explanation: Helping with a small inconvenience when a neighbour is away is a kind community gesture.

payload.snippet: You see two children from the street throwing stones at your neighbour's fence.
options: Tell a trusted adult what you saw
Join in
Shout at them yourself
Say nothing because they might bully you
payload.explanation: Telling a trusted adult about property damage is the right action — it's not telling tales, it's being responsible.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour's child falls off their bike right in front of you.
options: Check if they are hurt and help them up
Keep cycling past
Laugh and ride away
Go home and tell your parents later
payload.explanation: Stopping to help someone who has fallen is a basic act of kindness.

payload.snippet: The photo came out very dark.
options: Move to a brighter spot
Close the curtains
Take fewer photos
Put the camera away
payload.explanation: Photos taken in dark places are hard to see. More light makes them much better.

payload.snippet: The picture is all blurry.
options: Hold the camera very still and try again
Shake the camera more
Put a filter on
Make the photo smaller
payload.explanation: Blurry photos happen when the camera moves. Keeping still helps the camera capture a sharp image.

payload.snippet: Your finger is covering part of the lens.
options: Move your finger away from the lens
Keep your finger there
Take the photo anyway
Add a sticker over it
payload.explanation: Covering the lens blocks the view. Always check your fingers are clear before pressing the button.

payload.snippet: The sun is shining right into the camera lens.
options: Turn so the sun is behind you
Close your eyes and press the button
Take the photo straight into the sun
Put sunglasses on the camera
payload.explanation: Shooting into the sun makes photos very bright and hard to see. Keeping the sun behind you gives a much clearer picture.

payload.snippet: The dog keeps moving every time you press the button.
options: Wait until the dog is sitting still
Make the dog run faster
Take a photo of something else
Put the dog in a box
payload.explanation: Moving subjects come out blurry. Waiting for a still moment helps you get a sharp, clear photo.

payload.snippet: The photo shows the inside of your pocket.
options: Take the phone out properly and try again
Keep taking photos in your pocket
Use the front camera
Delete all photos
payload.explanation: Accidental pocket photos happen when the camera button is pressed by mistake. Taking the phone out first solves it.

payload.snippet: You want to take a photo of a rainbow but it is very far away.
options: Zoom in to make the rainbow look bigger
Run towards the rainbow
Only photograph the sky
Wait for another rainbow
payload.explanation: Zooming brings distant things closer in the frame so you can see them better in the photo.

payload.snippet: Your photo has a big shadow across it.
options: Move so your shadow does not fall on the subject
Make the shadow bigger
Add more shadows on purpose
Turn off the lights
payload.explanation: Shadows in photos can block the subject. Moving your position so the shadow falls elsewhere fixes it.

payload.snippet: The colours in the photo look orange and strange indoors.
options: Turn on more lights or open the curtains
Take the photo in the dark
Use only one light
Paint the room a different colour
payload.explanation: Indoor lights can make photos look orange. More daylight or brighter lights help colours look natural.

payload.snippet: You want a photo of your whole family but there is no one to press the button.
options: Use the timer setting so the camera takes the photo automatically
Leave one person out
Hold the camera very far away
Draw a photo instead
payload.explanation: The timer lets you set the camera down, get in position, and have the camera take the photo on its own.

payload.snippet: The photo has too many people's heads cut off at the top.
options: Step back further so everyone fits in the frame
Make the people shorter
Only photograph feet
Tilt the camera upside down
payload.explanation: Stepping back gives more room in the frame so everyone's head and body can fit into the picture.

payload.snippet: It is night time and everything looks black in the photo.
options: Turn on a light near the subject
Take photos only at night
Close your eyes to take the photo
Use the photo as a bookmark
payload.explanation: Cameras need light to capture an image. A nearby light source brightens the subject so it shows up clearly.

payload.snippet: You want a photo of a butterfly but it flies away before you can press the button.
options: Wait very quietly and still for the butterfly to land again
Chase the butterfly waving your arms
Take a photo of a flower instead
Give up and go inside
payload.explanation: Patience is important in nature photography. Staying quiet and still gives wild creatures time to settle.

payload.snippet: The photo has a big pole growing out of someone's head.
options: Move to a different angle where the pole is not behind the person
Cut the photo in half
Saw the pole down
Ignore it
payload.explanation: Distracting objects in the background can be removed simply by changing your position slightly.

payload.snippet: You take a photo of your drawing but the paper looks very white and bright.
options: Move to indirect light instead of direct sunshine
Draw on darker paper
Hold the drawing behind a curtain
Only photograph in the dark
payload.explanation: Direct sunlight bleaches out white paper. Soft indirect light preserves the colours and details of your drawing.

payload.snippet: Your selfie only shows the top of your head.
options: Hold the camera a little higher and tilt it down slightly
Take a photo of just your hair
Ask a friend to take it instead
Stand on a chair
payload.explanation: Holding the camera slightly above eye level and tilting it down creates a flattering angle that shows your whole face.

payload.snippet: The photo is too small to see the details of your model you built.
options: Move the camera closer to fill the frame with the model
Build a bigger model
Put the model far away
Use a smaller camera
payload.explanation: Getting closer to a subject fills the frame with detail, making it much easier to see in the finished photo.

payload.snippet: You want to photograph the moon but it looks like a tiny white dot.
options: Use as much zoom as possible and keep the camera very still
Throw the camera up in the air
Wait until the moon is bigger
Turn off the zoom
payload.explanation: The moon is very far away; maximum zoom combined with a very steady hold gets the best detail.

payload.snippet: Your birthday photo has red glowing eyes.
options: Turn off the flash and use a lamp nearby instead
Give everyone red-eye drops
Use a bigger flash
Add red sunglasses to the photo
payload.explanation: Red eye is caused by flash reflecting off the retina. Using ambient light instead of direct flash eliminates the effect.

payload.snippet: The background of the photo is very messy and distracting.
options: Move the subject to a cleaner spot or step closer to fill the frame
Add more mess to make it fair
Take the photo from below
Edit the background orange
payload.explanation: A clean or simple background keeps the viewer's attention on the subject rather than the clutter behind them.

payload.snippet: You are doing a puzzle and cannot find the last piece.
options: Look under the table and cushions where it might have fallen
Give up and throw the puzzle away
Colour in a piece of paper to replace it
Blame your brother
payload.explanation: Puzzle pieces often fall under furniture. Checking nearby surfaces and the floor is always worth a try.

payload.snippet: Two puzzle pieces look exactly the same but one does not fit.
options: Try both and use the one that clicks in smoothly
Force the wrong one in with your fist
Cut the piece to make it fit
Throw both away
payload.explanation: Similar-looking pieces are common in puzzles. Gently trying each one and feeling for the click tells you which is correct.

payload.snippet: You accidentally sit on one puzzle piece and it bends.
options: Gently flatten it under a heavy book
Throw it away immediately
Keep it bent so you know which one it is
Hide it at the back of the box
payload.explanation: A bent piece can often be flattened by placing something heavy on it for a few minutes.

payload.snippet: The puzzle box has a picture but the pieces are all face down.
options: Turn all the pieces face up before you start
Build the puzzle with the pieces face down
Put all the brown pieces together
Give up because you cannot see the picture
payload.explanation: Turning all pieces face up first gives you the whole picture to work with and makes it much easier to match shapes and colours.

payload.snippet: You are halfway done but need to go for dinner.
options: Leave the puzzle on the table and come back after dinner
Sweep it all back into the box
Take the puzzle to the dinner table
Ask your mum to finish it
payload.explanation: Leaving the puzzle where it is means you can carry on where you left off without losing your progress.

payload.snippet: You cannot tell which side is the right way up for one puzzle piece.
options: Compare it to the picture on the box to find the right orientation
Try all four ways until one looks right
Glue it in anyway
Skip that piece
payload.explanation: The box picture is your guide — comparing the colours and patterns on the piece to the picture quickly shows which way it should go.

payload.snippet: The puzzle is too big for the table.
options: Move to the floor where there is more space
Build only half the puzzle
Cut the board in half
Fold the puzzle up
payload.explanation: Large puzzles need lots of space. The floor gives you plenty of room to spread out and see all the pieces.

payload.snippet: A small child has chewed one puzzle piece and now it does not fit properly.
options: Contact the puzzle maker to ask for a replacement piece
Try forcing it in
Leave a gap in the puzzle
Put the chewed piece at the edge where gaps show less
payload.explanation: Many puzzle companies will send replacement pieces if you contact them. In the meantime, leaving the gap is better than forcing a damaged piece.

payload.snippet: You pick up a piece that looks like it should go in a gap but the colour is slightly wrong.
options: Set it aside and try other pieces first
Colour it in with a marker to match
Jam it in since it almost fits
Tear the hole bigger so it fits
payload.explanation: If a piece almost fits but the colour is off, it belongs somewhere else. Keeping it separate and coming back to it often finds the right spot.

payload.snippet: You have sorted all the edge pieces but now cannot find a corner.
options: Check for pieces that have two flat sides — those are the corners
Start in the middle instead
Assume there are no corners in this puzzle
Empty the box and start again
payload.explanation: Corner pieces are the only ones with two straight sides at a right angle. Looking specifically for that shape finds them quickly.

payload.snippet: The puzzle is of a blue sky and every piece looks the same blue.
options: Sort by the exact shade of blue and look at the shapes
Give up because all sky puzzles are impossible
Use only the edge pieces
Glue all the blue pieces together randomly
payload.explanation: Even a uniform sky has slight tonal and colour variations. Sorting by subtle shade differences, then matching the irregular shapes, is the key to tricky sky sections.

payload.snippet: You drop the puzzle from the table and all the pieces scatter.
options: Collect all the pieces and start sorting them again
Cry and refuse to start over
Glue whatever lands together
Decide the puzzle is done
payload.explanation: Accidents happen. Patiently collecting and re-sorting gives you a fresh start and you will often find pieces you missed before.

payload.snippet: One puzzle piece fits but leaves a visible white gap around its edges.
options: Remove it and keep looking — a slightly different piece will fill the gap completely
Accept the gap as part of the design
Fill the gap with white paint
Declare the puzzle finished anyway
payload.explanation: A visible gap means the piece is almost but not quite right. The correct piece will fit snugly with no gap showing.

payload.snippet: You want to do a puzzle but all the pieces are still in the bag from the shop.
options: Empty all the pieces onto the table first, then turn them face up
Try to build the puzzle with pieces still in the bag
Pour the pieces back into the box and use the box lid as a tray
Only take pieces out one at a time as you need them
payload.explanation: Emptying all pieces and turning them face up before starting gives you the full picture to work from and is much more efficient.

payload.snippet: Your puzzle picture shows a garden and you do not know where to start.
options: Find and build the straight-edged border first
Pick any piece from the middle and work outward
Sort by which pieces you like best

payload.explanation: Building the frame first gives you a defined shape and boundary that makes filling in the middle much easier.

payload.snippet: Two friends both want to do the same puzzle at the same time.
options: Agree to each work on a different section of the puzzle

Divide all the pieces into two equal piles

payload.explanation: Dividing the puzzle into sections lets both friends work simultaneously, making it go faster and keeping everyone involved.

payload.snippet: You have finished the puzzle but one piece is missing even after searching everywhere.

payload.explanation: One missing piece from a finished puzzle is a common experience. The work is still complete and worth celebrating. You can always look for the piece again later.

shout it's not fair
snatch her paper
rip her work
payload.explanation: Kind telling sorts copying.

payload.snippet: Your two friends both want to play your game.
options: let them both join in
pick a favourite only
leave one out always
play alone instead
payload.explanation: Both joining is fair.

payload.snippet: Your teacher gives the same prize to two pupils.
options: be happy for them
argue you should win
snatch the prize
moan about fairness
payload.explanation: Being happy is fair sport.

payload.snippet: Your friend always gets to choose the game.
options: say it's your turn to pick
sulk and play badly
let her always choose
leave the playground
payload.explanation: Taking turns is fair.

payload.snippet: Your sister wants the same toy as you.
options: set a five minute timer
hide the toy
tell mum on her
stamp on the toy
payload.explanation: Timers share toys fairly.

payload.snippet: Your brother says you have to share your sweets.
options: split them in two piles
eat them all fast
give him the gone-off ones
hide them in your bed
payload.explanation: Two piles is fair sharing.

payload.snippet: Your friend's snack looks much bigger than yours.
options: say it's fine and eat yours
snatch some of hers
moan to your friend
tip hers on the floor
payload.explanation: Eating yours is fair.

payload.snippet: Your mum says no telly for either of you tonight.
options: play a game with sister
argue with mum loudly
secretly watch alone
blame your sister
payload.explanation: Same rule for both is fair.

payload.snippet: Your friend got the seat by the window.
options: let her sit there today
push her out the seat
moan about windows
stand in her way
payload.explanation: Letting her sit is fair.

payload.snippet: Your team won the game by one goal.
options: shake hands with losers
brag about winning loudly
rub the win in their faces
kick the goalpost
payload.explanation: Handshakes are fair sport.

payload.snippet: Your sister did the worst of the chore.
options: swap chores next week
leave her with worst forever
swap if mum looks
moan about chores
payload.explanation: Swapping turns is fair.

payload.snippet: Your friend wants to be team captain again.
options: suggest taking turns to captain
let her captain always
fight her for it
leave the team
payload.explanation: Taking turns is fair leadership.

payload.snippet: Your dad gives you both the same pocket money.
options: say thank you to dad
ask for more than sister
snatch hers too
moan it's not enough
payload.explanation: Same amount is fair.

payload.snippet: Your friend wins pass the parcel today.
options: clap for her happily
sulk in the corner
snatch her prize
leave the party
payload.explanation: Clapping is fair celebration.

payload.snippet: Your mum splits the last biscuit in two.
options: take the half kindly
snatch both halves
moan it's tiny
feed it to the dog
payload.explanation: Halves are fair.

payload.snippet: Lena and Marco are building a model bridge. Lena wants to use tape; Marco wants glue. Neither will work if used at the wrong stage.
options: They discuss which method suits each part and use both
Lena uses tape on the whole bridge without asking Marco
Marco hides the glue so Lena cannot use tape
They give up and build separate bridges
payload.explanation: Combining approaches gives the best outcome when both have merit.

payload.snippet: The school's garden group has to dig, plant, and water. There are three children and three jobs.
options: They each take one job and work at the same time
One child does all three jobs while the others watch
They all try to water the same plant at once
They argue about which job is best for twenty minutes
payload.explanation: Parallel task division gets work done three times as fast.

payload.snippet: Ava's team is behind in a spelling relay. She misspells a word and feels terrible.
options: Her teammates tell her not to worry and cheer her on
Her teammates blame her for losing the round
Ava sits down and refuses to continue
Her teammates ask the teacher to swap Ava out
payload.explanation: Positive team responses to mistakes keep morale and performance up.

payload.snippet: In an art project, Josh is good at drawing and Priya is good at colouring. Their teacher asks them to pair up.
options: Josh draws the outline and Priya fills it in
Josh draws and colours the whole thing because he thinks he is better
Priya redraws Josh's outline because she dislikes his style
They submit two separate pieces instead of one together
payload.explanation: Assigning roles by strength produces better combined output.

payload.snippet: Ben and Sam are building a sandcastle. Ben builds towers quickly but sloppily; Sam builds slowly but solidly.
options: Ben builds quickly and Sam strengthens each tower behind him
Ben knocks Sam's careful towers over saying they are too slow
Sam redoes every tower Ben has made
They compete to see whose towers last longer
payload.explanation: Complementary working speeds can be an asset when coordinated.

payload.snippet: A team quiz needs a captain who buzzes in. Three players all want to buzz and keep pressing at once.
options: They agree one person will buzz only when they all nod
They all buzz simultaneously and shout over each other
The fastest presser always buzzes and the others give up
They take turns buzzing regardless of who knows the answer
payload.explanation: A shared signal system prevents simultaneous buzzing and wins more rounds.

payload.snippet: Two friends are moving chairs for a school assembly. Carrying one each is slow; carrying two together is much faster.
options: They carry two chairs each by working together on the awkward ones
They carry one each and make many slow trips
One carries all the chairs to show off their strength
They push the chairs along the floor rather than carrying them
payload.explanation: Cooperating on the awkward-shaped items speeds up the whole job.

payload.snippet: Ella's role in the group is keeping time. She forgets to start the timer and the team loses a point.
options: The team accepts the mistake, resets, and checks the timer is running before starting again
The team argues about whose fault it was and misses the next round too
Ella is removed as timekeeper without being told why
The team refuses to continue the activity
payload.explanation: A calm procedural reset after a mistake prevents one error from snowballing.

payload.snippet: Two classmates are doing a science experiment together. One wants to test quickly; the other wants to record every step.
options: They agree: test quickly but pause at each step to record before moving on
The quick tester skips ahead and the recorder misses steps
The recorder insists on writing three paragraphs per step, exhausting them both
They split the experiment into two individual experiments
payload.explanation: Negotiating a pace that satisfies both the doer and the recorder produces reliable results.

payload.snippet: In a group cooking class, one child measures and one child mixes. The measurer keeps adding too much.
options: The mixer gently tells the measurer to double-check the measurement before adding
The mixer says nothing and the recipe is ruined
The measurer is removed from the task for adding wrong amounts
The mixer takes over both jobs without explaining why
payload.explanation: Constructive real-time feedback between teammates catches errors before they compound.

payload.snippet: Tom's football team is losing 3–0. Some players say it is pointless to keep trying.
options: The captain encourages the team to play their best regardless of the score
The team starts kicking wildly and the score becomes 5–0
Half the team gives up and walks to the side of the pitch
Players start blaming each other for the goals conceded
payload.explanation: Team spirit and effort have value even when a result is unlikely to change.

payload.snippet: Zara and Noah are doing a three-legged race. They keep tripping because they start on different feet.
options: They stop, agree on which foot to start with, and try again
Zara drags Noah forward so she can control the pace
Noah keeps changing feet hoping it will improve
They blame each other and refuse to continue
payload.explanation: A brief stop to synchronise is faster than continuing with the wrong method.

payload.snippet: The class mural project has no leader and everyone paints whatever they want. The mural is becoming chaotic.
options: The class pauses, agrees a rough plan, and assigns sections
The teacher paints the whole mural to rescue it
The class continues and later argues about the mess
The loudest student takes over and overpaints everyone else's work
payload.explanation: A brief planning pause rescues an uncoordinated group effort.

payload.snippet: Maya's group project is due tomorrow. One group member has not done their part and is not responding to messages.
options: The group tells their teacher and asks for guidance on how to proceed fairly
The group submits the project without that section and blames the absent member
The group does the member's part and pretends they all did equal work
The group delays submission without notifying the teacher
payload.explanation: Escalating a collaboration problem to a teacher before a deadline protects the whole group.

payload.snippet: Two children are raking leaves into a pile. One child keeps scattering leaves as they drag the rake.
options: They discuss technique and angle the rake to gather, not scatter
The tidy raker insults the scatterer's method
They work in opposite directions making equal piles
The scatterer gives up and watches
payload.explanation: Shared techniques for team tasks improve collective efficiency.

payload.snippet: In a gym class relay, the fastest runner wants to go last but the current order puts her first.
options: The team agrees the strategy: fastest last to close the gap if needed
The fastest runner goes last without telling anyone, disrupting the order
The team refuses to change the order even if it costs them the race
The fast runner runs every leg herself
payload.explanation: Agreeing strategy openly rather than acting unilaterally is how teams optimise.

payload.snippet: A pair project requires a written and a spoken section. One partner hates speaking aloud; the other hates writing.
options: They agree: the stronger writer writes and the stronger speaker presents
They each do both sections badly rather than play to strengths
One partner does everything because neither wants to compromise
They tell the teacher the project is impossible with this partner
payload.explanation: Voluntarily taking the role you are better at is good team sense.

payload.snippet: During a team obstacle course, one child is much slower at climbing. The rest of the team must wait.
options: The team cheers the slower climber and offers tips while they wait
The rest of the team rushes ahead and the climber falls behind
The team complains to the teacher that the climber is slowing them down
The team tries to carry the climber up the obstacle
payload.explanation: Patient encouragement of the slowest teammate keeps the whole team functioning.

payload.snippet: After a project, two students take credit in front of the teacher while the third is not mentioned.
options: The third student tells the teacher they also contributed and lists what they did
The third student says nothing but feels resentful
The third student refuses to do any group work in future
The third student confronts the other two angrily at lunch
payload.explanation: Claiming your own credit calmly is fair and does not require drama.

payload.snippet: Two children are supposed to clean the classroom together but one keeps checking their phone.
options: The attentive child asks the other to put the phone down so they can finish together
The attentive child cleans everything alone and resents the other
Both children end up on their phones and the room stays dirty
The attentive child tells the teacher the other is not helping
payload.explanation: A direct, friendly request to refocus is faster and kinder than silent resentment.

payload.snippet: Jake has been waiting for a parcel for five days. Every day he checks the door and feels disappointed.
options: He checks the tracking link once a day and does other things while he waits
He emails the company every hour asking for updates
He goes to the delivery depot without being told it is there
He gives up waiting and asks for a refund after two days
payload.explanation: Tracking links give up-to-date information — hourly emails achieve nothing and cause stress.

payload.snippet: Priya is learning to play the piano. After two lessons she says she will never be good enough.
options: Her teacher reminds her that all skills take time and she plays back her very first attempt to show progress
Her teacher tells her she is right and switches to a simpler instrument
Priya's parents allow her to quit after only two lessons
Priya practises for twelve hours straight hoping to speed up her progress
payload.explanation: Comparing early progress to beginners, not experts, makes patience easier.

payload.snippet: Oliver is waiting in a long queue at the theme park. The ride is forty-five minutes away.
options: He chats to his family and watches people on the ride
He pushes to the front claiming he was there earlier
He leaves the queue and sulks on a bench
He complains to staff every five minutes
payload.explanation: Making the wait enjoyable with conversation shortens perceived waiting time.

payload.snippet: Ava bakes cupcakes and wants to ice them but they are still warm. Icing will melt.
options: She waits twenty minutes for them to cool on a wire rack
She puts icing on immediately and watches it melt and slide
She puts them in the freezer for one minute and then ices them immediately
She puts them in a bag and gives them to friends unattempted
payload.explanation: Cooling completely before icing is the difference between a neat result and a mess.

payload.snippet: Riya is learning to swim. After three lessons she can only float. She wants to quit.
options: Her instructor shows her a video of beginners from the same week and points out she is already floating, which took most students longer
Her instructor lets her drop the lessons without any discussion
Riya's parents tell her all children swim perfectly after three lessons
Riya practises twenty lengths at home in the bath
payload.explanation: Benchmarking against realistic comparisons makes patience with learning curves sustainable.

payload.snippet: Leo has saved up for a new game for eight weeks. When he arrives at the shop the game is sold out and will be back in stock in three days.
options: He asks the shop to hold a copy and comes back in three days
He buys a different game he doesn't want just to have something
He demands the shop restock immediately
He searches every shop in the city that day
payload.explanation: Three days is a short wait for the right item — reserving it guarantees success.

payload.snippet: Maya sends a message to a new friend asking to meet up. Two hours pass with no reply.
options: She does something else and checks her phone later
She sends ten follow-up messages in quick succession
She decides the friend doesn't like her and deletes their number
She calls the friend's house phone
payload.explanation: Doubling down on unanswered messages makes people less likely to respond, not more.

payload.snippet: Ben is on a long car journey. He asks 'are we nearly there yet?' every ten minutes.
options: He plays a car game with the family to make the journey feel shorter
He cries for the last hour of the journey
He demands they stop the car immediately
He opens the car door to check how far they have gone
payload.explanation: Engaged activities transform a long wait into an enjoyable experience.

payload.snippet: Chloe is waiting for her turn to use the art room printer. Three people are ahead of her and each print takes five minutes.
options: She prepares her work fully while she waits so she is ready the moment it is her turn
She hovers over the printer making others uncomfortable
She tells the teacher the others should let her go first
She prints on the office printer without asking
payload.explanation: Using the wait productively means no extra delay when it is finally her turn.

payload.snippet: Tom is learning to juggle. He keeps dropping the balls after two catches. He's been practising for a week.
options: He asks his teacher if there is a simpler progression — starting with one ball then two — before three
He throws all three balls away in frustration
He practises nonstop for three hours and injures his wrist
He tells everyone juggling is impossible
payload.explanation: Breaking a skill into smaller stages shortens the perceived wait for mastery.

payload.snippet: Sam's vegetable garden has seeds he planted last month. Nothing visible has appeared.
options: He checks the soil moisture and continues watering on schedule
He digs up the seeds to see if they have sprouted
He replants completely different seeds
He pours extra fertiliser on in large quantities to accelerate growth
payload.explanation: Seeds work underground for weeks before surface signs appear — patience and consistent care are all that is needed.

payload.snippet: Freya is waiting for a doctor's appointment running thirty minutes late. She is anxious about the wait.
options: She reads a book she brought and tells the receptionist she will need to leave by a fixed time
She leaves without being seen and feels worse at home
She repeatedly asks the receptionist how much longer
She pushes into an occupied consultation room
payload.explanation: Bringing something to occupy the wait and calmly flagging a time constraint is both patient and practical.

payload.snippet: Noah waits for his friend to finish a phone call so they can play. The call goes on for fifteen minutes.
options: He finds something to do quietly while he waits
He hangs up the friend's phone for them
He makes loud noises to hurry the call
He leaves without saying anything
payload.explanation: Occupying yourself calmly during someone else's obligation is basic courtesy.

payload.snippet: Zara is very excited about a surprise but she was told not to open it until her birthday in two days.
options: She asks her mum to hide it somewhere she won't see it so the temptation is reduced
She opens it then pretends it is still wrapped
She shakes it to work out what it is
She tells her friends what she thinks it is, ruining her own excitement
payload.explanation: Removing visual temptation is a practical patience strategy.

payload.snippet: Jonah's club meeting is delayed by thirty minutes because the room is being used for an exam.
options: He chats with other club members outside and reviews the meeting agenda
He knocks on the exam room door to hurry them along
He goes home and misses the meeting
He rearranges all the chairs in the corridor
payload.explanation: A delay is an opportunity to prepare for the meeting, not a crisis.

payload.snippet: Mia is waiting for a birthday present she ordered herself to arrive. She already knows what it is since she chose it.
options: She does other things and checks the delivery notification when it comes
She opens the door every time a car goes past
She texts the shop every few hours for an update
She cancels the order and goes to buy it in person immediately
payload.explanation: Tracking notifications make doorstep vigils unnecessary — living normally is how waiting passes fastest.

payload.snippet: Ben and his dad are fishing. After an hour nothing has bitten. Dad says they need patience.
options: Ben watches the water quietly and enjoys being outside
He shouts at the water to scare fish toward the hook
He throws extra bread in to make fishing easier
He tells Dad fishing is boring after ten minutes
payload.explanation: Fishing teaches patience — the waiting is as much the activity as the catching.

payload.snippet: Olivia queues for a popular school lunch. The queue moves slowly and she is hungry.
options: She chats with her friend and waits her turn calmly
She cuts the line because she is very hungry
She complains loudly every minute
She leaves the queue and goes hungry to make a point
payload.explanation: Being hungry makes queuing harder — chatting makes the wait feel shorter.

payload.snippet: Tom is waiting for his turn to use the school computer. Two people are ahead of him.
options: He reads his book until the computer is free
He stands behind the computer user making them nervous
He asks the teacher to make the others hurry
He uses another student's unsaved work so he can start
payload.explanation: Reading while waiting is the classic patience strategy.

payload.snippet: Nora has been learning to whistle for two days and still cannot do it.
options: She keeps trying for five minutes each day
She gives up and says she will never be able to whistle
She asks an adult to whistle for her instead
She blows so hard she goes dizzy
payload.explanation: Small daily practice with rest between sessions is how new physical skills develop.

payload.snippet: Jake is cycling to school and his helmet strap is too loose. He can wobble the helmet with one finger.
options: He stops and adjusts the strap so the helmet fits snugly under his chin
He cycles on since the helmet is still on his head
He removes the helmet and puts it in his bag
He holds the helmet on with one hand while steering with the other
payload.explanation: A loose helmet won't protect your head in a crash — fit must be checked before riding.

payload.snippet: Ava is cooking pasta and the pot of boiling water starts to steam badly near her face.
options: She steps back and uses the pan handle to keep distance while stirring
She leans in close to check the pasta is cooking
She turns the hob to full power to cook it faster
She removes the lid by grabbing the glass part
payload.explanation: Steam burns are as serious as direct flame burns — stay back and use the handle.

payload.snippet: Oliver finds a door left open to the road while playing in his front garden.
options: He tells a parent and stays inside until the door is closed
He goes out through the door to explore
He waves to cars hoping they see him
He closes the door himself by pushing hard
payload.explanation: An open gate to a road is a significant safety hazard for children — tell an adult.

payload.snippet: Priya is at the beach and a rip current sign is posted at the entry point.
options: She shows the sign to her parent before entering the water
She swims in the area because the water looks calm
She wades up to her knees since she won't go further
She swims parallel to the shore in the rip current zone
payload.explanation: Rip current warnings must be heeded regardless of how calm the water appears.

payload.snippet: Ben is helping his dad in the garage and spots a container of petrol with no lid.
options: He tells his dad the lid is missing before they do anything else
He sniffs the container to check it is petrol
He puts a cloth over the container as a temporary lid
He kicks the container gently to see how full it is
payload.explanation: Uncapped petrol vapour is highly flammable — an adult must secure it immediately.

payload.snippet: Lily is home alone when she smells smoke coming from upstairs.
options: She leaves the house immediately without investigating and calls 999 from outside
She goes upstairs to find the source of the smoke
She opens windows to clear the smoke
She calls her mum before leaving the house
payload.explanation: In a fire, speed of exit matters more than investigation — call 999 from outside.

payload.snippet: Noah is on a hike and twists his ankle badly. The group is thirty minutes from the trailhead.
options: He tells the group leader and they assess whether he can walk or needs assistance
He walks on without telling anyone so the group doesn't have to stop
He sits down alone and tells the group to go ahead
He tries to run back to the car to get there faster
payload.explanation: Reporting an injury to the group leader allows a proper safety assessment and support.

payload.snippet: Chloe is playing at the park when a child she does not know falls and bangs their head on the equipment.
options: She tells a nearby adult immediately
She tells the child they will be fine and keeps playing
She tries to help the child up quickly
She watches to see if the child cries before deciding to act
payload.explanation: A head injury in a child always requires adult assessment — don't delay.

payload.snippet: Tom sees his younger sibling about to put a coin in their mouth.
options: He takes the coin gently but firmly and calls a parent
He laughs and tells his parents later
He lets his sibling have the coin since it is just a small one
He taps his sibling on the head to startle them
payload.explanation: Coins are choking hazards for young children — calm intervention and adult alert is the right response.

payload.snippet: Zara is at a fireworks display. Someone is lighting hand-held sparklers for children. She has no gloves.
options: She asks for gardening gloves or folded paper to hold the sparkler handle
She holds the sparkler at the very end near the wire
She holds it close to the sparkle so she can see it better
She holds it without anything since it looks cool
payload.explanation: Sparklers burn at extreme temperatures — hand protection and arm's-length holding are essential.

payload.snippet: Maya notices the playground climbing frame has a broken rung.
options: She tells a teacher and keeps others away from that section
She climbs the frame avoiding the broken rung
She tells her friend not to use that rung but says nothing to adults
She tries to fix the rung with a stick
payload.explanation: Broken playground equipment must be reported to adults so it can be made safe or cordoned off.

payload.snippet: Felix is learning to use a kitchen knife. He places the knife on the bench with the blade pointing toward him.
options: He turns the knife so the blade points away from him and the handle faces toward him
He keeps the knife pointing toward him since it is closer
He puts the knife in a drawer blade-up so it is easier to grab
He carries the knife to the sink blade-up
payload.explanation: Blades should always point away from the body and away from the aisle when stored on a bench.

payload.snippet: Ellie is swimming in a river on a warm day. There are no warning signs but the water looks dark and deep.
options: She stays in the shallow edge where she can stand
She dives in from the bank to cool down quickly
She swims to the middle to show off to her friends
She jumps off a rock into the deep part
payload.explanation: Unknown river depth and currents make deep water dangerous even without warning signs.

payload.snippet: A student notices a frayed electrical cable on the classroom projector.
options: She tells the teacher immediately and suggests no one touch it
She wraps the frayed section with sellotape to make it safe temporarily
She unplugs the projector herself
She tells another student to tell the teacher
payload.explanation: Frayed cables are an electrocution and fire risk — report to a responsible adult immediately.

payload.snippet: Oscar is making popcorn on the hob and the oil starts to smoke heavily.
options: He turns off the heat and covers the pan with a lid, then steps back
He throws water on the smoking oil
He moves the pan to the sink
He blows on the pan to cool it down
payload.explanation: Water and hot oil cause fireball explosions — covering with a lid smothers the heat safely.

payload.snippet: During a school trip, Riya gets separated from her group in a shopping centre.
options: She finds a member of staff at a service desk and tells them her school name and teacher's name
She walks around looking for her group for an hour
She leaves the shopping centre to look outside
She calls her mum and waits at the exit
payload.explanation: A service desk or security point is the safest place for a separated child to wait and get help.

payload.snippet: Ben's friend dares him to balance on the roof of a low outbuilding. The tiles look mossy.
options: He refuses and suggests a different challenge
He climbs up slowly and carefully
He goes up but stays very still in the middle
He takes off his shoes for better grip
payload.explanation: Mossy tiles are extremely slippery — refusing a dangerous dare is always the right call.

payload.snippet: Two children are playing near a frozen pond. One steps onto the ice.
options: The child on the ice is called back to the bank immediately
They both step onto the ice since it looks thick enough
They test the ice by jumping on it
They throw a rock to test the ice strength
payload.explanation: Ice thickness cannot be reliably assessed by sight — no one should step on a frozen pond.

payload.snippet: Mia notices her friend is not wearing a seatbelt in the back seat.
options: She asks her friend to put the seatbelt on before the car moves
She tells her friend once and lets it go when she refuses
She ignores it since her friend is in the back seat
She pulls the seatbelt across for her friend without asking
payload.explanation: Seatbelts save lives in all seats — asking a friend to buckle up is looking out for them.

payload.snippet: Sam finds a lighter on the floor of the park.
options: He picks it up by the sides, does not operate it, and gives it to an adult
He tries to light it to see if it works
He throws it in a bin near dry grass
He keeps it in his pocket to show his friends
payload.explanation: Lighters are fire hazards especially near dry vegetation — give to an adult promptly.

payload.snippet: Jake finishes a bottle of ketchup. There is still a little ketchup stuck inside.
options: He rinses the bottle before putting it in the recycling
He puts it in recycling with ketchup inside since it's only a little
He throws it in the general bin because it's hard to clean
He leaves it on the counter for weeks
payload.explanation: Residual food contaminates recycling — a quick rinse solves the problem.

payload.snippet: Ava's family has a pile of broken electronics: an old phone, a toaster, and a tablet.
options: She takes them to the council's electrical recycling drop-off point
She puts them all in the general bin
She puts them in the kerbside recycling
She throws them in the back garden
payload.explanation: Electrical items contain hazardous materials — they must go to designated e-waste points.

payload.snippet: Oliver finds that his family puts all their recycling in one unsorted bin. His council requires separate bins for different materials.
options: He creates labels for each bin so every family member knows what goes where
He sorts through all the bins every week alone without telling anyone
He ignores the sorting requirement since his family won't change
He asks his mum to throw everything in the general bin
payload.explanation: Labelling bins reduces sorting errors — one labelled system change benefits the whole household.

payload.snippet: Priya's school has a fundraiser: collecting bottle caps for charity. She keeps forgetting to save them.
options: She puts a small box near the recycling bin to collect caps before they go in
She goes through the bin each evening to retrieve thrown-away caps
She asks her whole class to save caps but does none herself
She gives up and donates money instead
payload.explanation: A collection point at the action location eliminates the forgetting problem.

payload.snippet: Ben's family orders a lot of online deliveries. Bubble wrap piles up every week.
options: He takes bubble wrap to the supermarket's carrier-bag and soft-plastic recycling point
He puts it in kerbside recycling where it jams the machinery
He burns it in the garden
He throws it all in the general bin
payload.explanation: Soft plastics like bubble wrap clog standard recycling machinery — only specialist soft-plastic points can process them.

payload.snippet: Lily finds a pile of old clothes that are worn out and cannot be donated.
options: She puts them in a textile recycling bank or her council's textile collection
She burns them in the garden
She puts them in the general bin
She leaves them in bags on the pavement
payload.explanation: Worn clothing can be recycled into industrial rags or insulation even if it cannot be donated.

payload.snippet: Noah buys a new appliance. It comes in a large polystyrene box.
options: He contacts the retailer or council to find specialist polystyrene recycling
He puts it in the kerbside recycling where it breaks into small beads
He burns it on the garden bonfire
He shoves it in the general bin
payload.explanation: Polystyrene is not collected in standard kerbside recycling and releases toxic gases if burned.

payload.snippet: Chloe has old cooking oil from the chip pan. The council leaflet says it must not go down the drain.
options: She lets it cool, pours it into a sealed container, and takes it to a cooking-oil recycling collection
She pours it down the drain slowly
She pours it on the garden compost
She puts it in the general bin while still liquid
payload.explanation: Cooking oil poured down drains causes fatbergs — cooking-oil recycling converts it to biofuel.

payload.snippet: Tom finishes a tube of toothpaste. He has read that mixed-material tubes are hard to recycle.
options: He checks whether his toothpaste brand offers a free recycling scheme through a recycling programme
He puts it in the plastic recycling since it looks like plastic
He puts it in the general bin without checking
He crushes it to a smaller size and puts it in kerbside recycling
payload.explanation: Many toothpaste brands partner with specialist recycling schemes specifically for mixed-material tubes.

payload.snippet: Zara and her family finish a case of bottled water. They want to reduce their plastic use going forward.
options: She proposes the family switch to a filtered water jug and reusable bottles
She recycles the plastic bottles and continues buying single-use water
She throws the bottles away since recycling takes effort
She fills old bottles with tap water without cleaning them
payload.explanation: The most impactful recycling action is reducing the production of waste in the first place.

payload.snippet: Maya has finished a packet of crisps. The metalised packet is not accepted in kerbside recycling.
options: She puts the packet in a specialist crisp-packet collection scheme at a supermarket
She puts it in kerbside plastic recycling since it looks like plastic
She puts it in the general bin without checking alternatives
She washes and irons it flat to use as wrapping paper
payload.explanation: Metalised film packets require specialist processing unavailable in standard kerbside collections.

payload.snippet: Felix has old ink cartridges from his printer. His council does not collect them.
options: He returns them to a supermarket or office supply store that takes used cartridges
He puts them in the general bin
He puts them in kerbside recycling since they are plastic
He leaves them on the pavement outside the recycling bins
payload.explanation: Printer cartridges contain ink residue and mixed materials — manufacturer take-back schemes process them correctly.

payload.snippet: Ellie has finished a bottle of sunscreen. She is unsure whether the tube and pump are recyclable separately.
options: She separates the pump mechanism, checks both on her council's website, and recycles each in the correct bin
She puts the whole thing in plastic recycling since sunscreen bottles look like plastic
She throws it all in the general bin to save time
She washes the bottle and reuses it for shampoo
payload.explanation: Pump dispensers are often made of multiple materials — checking each component separately gives the best outcome.

payload.snippet: Oscar's family has a pile of old mobile phones in a drawer that no one uses.
options: He researches whether charities accept working phones and takes broken ones to an e-waste bin at a supermarket
He puts them in the general bin
He leaves them in the drawer forever
He puts them in kerbside recycling
payload.explanation: Working phones can be donated to domestic abuse charities; broken ones must go to e-waste not general waste.

payload.snippet: Riya's school canteen produces food waste. The school bins everything together.
options: She raises it with the school council and asks whether a compost collection can be arranged
She ignores it since the school is responsible for its own waste
She collects food scraps herself and takes them home
She tells her teacher the bins are too full
payload.explanation: Student advocacy through school councils is how waste systems in schools get changed.

payload.snippet: Ben notices his neighbours put their bins out on the wrong day and missed the collection. Bags are left on the pavement.
options: He knocks and lets them know when the next collection day is and what is accepted
He ignores it since it is their responsibility
He adds his recycling to their pile on the pavement
He reports them to the council for incorrect binning
payload.explanation: A neighbourly reminder prevents a week of littering and helps both households manage waste correctly.

payload.snippet: Two friends argue about whether a grease-stained pizza box can be recycled.
options: They agree to compost the greasy bottom section and recycle the clean lid
One throws the whole box in recycling to win the argument
They both put it in the general bin to settle the dispute
They leave it out while they research for three hours
payload.explanation: Splitting a box along the clean and greasy sections is the practical correct solution.

payload.snippet: Ella has a broken umbrella made of mixed materials: metal, fabric, and plastic.
options: She separates the components and recycles each in the correct stream where possible
She puts the whole umbrella in general bin
She puts it all in metal recycling since it has a metal frame
She leaves it near the recycling bins hoping someone else will sort it
payload.explanation: Mixed-material items should be disassembled — each component often has its own recyclable stream.

payload.snippet: Sofia finds a stack of old birthday and Christmas cards. Some have glitter, foil, or plastic windows.
options: She separates plain cards for paper recycling and puts glittered or foil ones in the general bin
She puts all cards in paper recycling since they are mostly paper
She burns them all in the garden
She puts them all in the general bin since sorting is complicated
payload.explanation: Glitter and foil contaminate paper recycling — sorting cards by finish is a quick and effective step.

payload.snippet: Alex's family has been putting batteries in the general bin. He reads they should not go in kerbside recycling.
options: He collects spent batteries in a small tub and drops them at the supermarket battery collection point
He continues putting them in the general bin since everyone does it
He puts them in kerbside recycling since they are a small item
He leaves them in a drawer until he forgets about them
payload.explanation: Batteries contain heavy metals and can cause fires in waste trucks — designated collection points are available in most supermarkets.

payload.snippet: Jake is baking bread for the first time. The recipe says knead for ten minutes but his arms are tired after five.
options: He asks his dad to take over for a few minutes then finishes himself
He stops kneading after five minutes and bakes it anyway
He uses the electric mixer on full speed hoping it is the same
He adds extra water to soften the dough so it needs less kneading
payload.explanation: Under-kneaded bread does not rise properly — dividing the work still achieves the full time.

payload.snippet: Ava is making cupcakes and realises she has no baking powder. She has bicarbonate of soda.
options: She searches online for how much bicarb to use as a substitute
She uses the same amount of bicarb as baking powder called for
She skips the leavening agent entirely
She adds twice the amount of bicarb to be safe
payload.explanation: Bicarb is three times stronger than baking powder — using the same amount produces a soapy taste.

payload.snippet: Oliver is making bread. He puts the dough in a warm spot to prove but it has barely risen after two hours.
options: He checks whether the yeast was still in date and if the water was too hot when added
He puts the dough in the oven immediately to force it to rise while baking
He adds more yeast on top of the already-proved dough
He kneads the dough again and starts the prove from scratch
payload.explanation: Yeast killed by hot water or past its date won't activate — diagnosing the cause determines the fix.

payload.snippet: Priya is baking biscuits and her oven runs hot. The first batch burns on the bottom while the top looks underdone.
options: She lowers the temperature, moves the tray to a higher shelf, and checks earlier next time
She removes the burned bottoms with a grater and re-ices the tops
She turns the oven up to cook the tops faster
She accepts burnt bottoms as normal for her oven
payload.explanation: Oven calibration affects all baking — adapting temperature and rack position corrects for a hot oven.

payload.snippet: Ben is making a sponge cake. He creams the butter and sugar but does not have an electric mixer, only a wooden spoon.
options: He creams by beating firmly for eight to ten minutes until pale and fluffy
He melts the butter and stirs it in with sugar quickly
He uses a fork which takes no extra effort
He skips creaming and mixes all ingredients together at once
payload.explanation: Creaming incorporates air for lift — it takes time by hand but cannot be skipped without affecting texture.

payload.snippet: Lily finds that her shortbread dough is very crumbly and won't stay together.
options: She adds a teaspoon of cold water and works it in gently until the dough just holds
She adds more butter until the dough feels wet
She adds a whole egg to bind it
She gives up and uses shop-bought biscuit dough
payload.explanation: Shortbread needs just enough liquid to bind — a teaspoon of cold water is the classic fix for crumbly dough.

payload.snippet: Noah is making a meringue. He notices a small amount of egg yolk got into his whites when separating them.
options: He carefully lifts the yolk out with a piece of shell and starts whipping immediately
He whips the whites including the yolk since it is only a tiny amount
He throws the whites away and starts again with fresh eggs
He adds cream of tartar which will neutralise the fat from the yolk
payload.explanation: Even a trace of fat from egg yolk prevents whites from whipping to full stiffness — remove it before whipping.

payload.snippet: Chloe follows a recipe that calls for plain flour but only has self-raising flour.
options: She uses self-raising flour and reduces any baking powder in the recipe to compensate
She uses the same amount of self-raising flour and the same amount of baking powder
She uses the self-raising flour and adds extra baking powder for more rise
She cannot make the recipe until she buys plain flour
payload.explanation: Self-raising flour already contains raising agents — using it without reducing the baking powder causes over-rising and collapse.

payload.snippet: Tom is making a Victoria sponge. He only has one cake tin but the recipe makes two layers.
options: He bakes the batter in two batches and allows the tin to cool between uses
He pours all the batter into the single tin to make a thick single-layer cake
He tries to bake both layers in the same tin separated by baking paper
He halves the recipe without adjusting baking time
payload.explanation: Two batches in one tin is slower but produces the correct layers — adjusting a recipe changes more than just quantities.

payload.snippet: Zara is making a chocolate cake and the ganache topping is too thick to pour smoothly.
options: She warms the ganache gently over a pan of hot water to thin it
She adds milk to thin it quickly
She puts it in the microwave on full power for two minutes
She spreads it as a thick paste with a spatula
payload.explanation: Gentle warming over water restores pourability without splitting the ganache.

payload.snippet: Maya is making pastry. Her kitchen is warm and the butter keeps melting into the flour too fast.
options: She chills the bowl, butter, and her hands in ice water before rubbing in
She uses room temperature butter since it is easier to work in
She adds more flour to compensate for the melting butter
She puts the finished pastry back in the freezer for one hour before rolling
payload.explanation: Cold ingredients and cold hands are essential for short pastry — warm kitchens require extra cooling steps.

payload.snippet: Felix is baking a loaf and the top crust is browning too fast before the inside is cooked.
options: He loosely tents the top with foil for the remaining baking time
He opens the oven every few minutes to check, which drops the temperature
